title: The Salad
paragraphs: A cheerful young huntsman was walking briskly through a wood when a little old woman came up to him and said, “Good day, good day. You look cheerful enough, but I am hungry and thirsty. Please give me something to eat.” The huntsman felt sorry for her, reached into his pocket, and gave her what he had. Then he wanted to be on his way, but she held on to him and said, “Listen, my friend, to what I’m about to tell you. I will repay you for your kindness. Go on your way, and after a while you will come to a tree where nine birds sit on a cloak. Shoot into the middle of them and one will fall down dead, and the cloak will fall with it. Take it. It is a wishing-cloak, and when you wear it you will find yourself at any place you wish to be. Cut open the dead bird, take out its heart, and keep it, and every morning when you get up you will find a piece of gold under your pillow. It is the bird’s heart that will bring you this good luck.”

The huntsman thanked her and thought to himself, “If all this really happens, it will be a fine thing for me.” After about a hundred steps he heard screeching and chirping in the branches above him. He looked up and saw a flock of birds pulling at a cloak with their beaks and claws, screaming, fighting, and tugging at one another as if each wanted it for himself. “Well,” said the huntsman, “this is amazing. It’s happening just as the old woman said.” Then he shot into the middle of them, so that feathers flew everywhere. The flock flew off, chattering, but one bird fell down dead, and the cloak with it. Then the huntsman did as the old woman had told him: he cut open the bird, took out the heart, and carried the cloak home with him.

The next morning when he woke up, he lifted his pillow, and there lay the piece of gold, glittering underneath. The same thing happened the next day, and in fact every day when he got up. He piled up a great deal of gold, and finally he thought to himself, “What good is this gold to me while I stay at home? I’ll go out into the world and have a look around.”

So he said goodbye to his friends, hung his bag and bow around his neck, and went on his way. One day it happened that his road led through a thick wood, and at the end of it stood a large castle in a green meadow. At one of the windows an old woman stood looking out, with a very beautiful young lady beside her. The old woman was a witch, and she said to the young lady, “There’s a young man coming out of the wood who is carrying a wonderful prize. We must get it away from him, my dear child, because it suits us better than it suits him. He has a bird’s heart that brings a piece of gold under his pillow every morning.” Meanwhile the huntsman came closer, looked at the lady, and said to himself, “I’ve been traveling so long that I’d like to go into this castle and rest, since I have money enough to pay for anything I need.” But the real reason was that he wanted to see more of the beautiful lady. So he went into the house and was kindly welcomed, and before long he was so much in love that he thought of nothing but gazing into the lady’s eyes and doing whatever she wished. Then the old woman said, “Now is the time to get the bird’s heart.” So the lady stole it from him, and he never found any more gold under his pillow, because it now lay under the young lady’s, and the old woman took it away every morning. But he was so much in love that he never missed his prize.

“Well,” said the old witch, “we have the bird’s heart, but not the wishing-cloak yet, and we have to get that too.” “Let’s leave him that,” said the young lady. “He has already lost his wealth.” The witch grew very angry and said, “A cloak like that is a rare and wonderful thing, and I must and will have it.” So she did as the old woman told her: she sat down at the window, looked out over the countryside, and seemed very sad. The huntsman asked, “Why are you so sad?” “Alas, dear sir,” she said, “over there lies the granite rock where all the precious diamonds grow. I want so badly to go there that whenever I think of it I can’t help being sad. But who can get there? Only the birds and the flies. Man cannot.” “If that’s all that troubles you,” said the huntsman, “I’ll gladly take you there.” So he drew her under his cloak, and the moment he wished to be on the granite mountain, they were both there. The diamonds glittered so on every side that they were delighted by the sight and picked up the finest ones. But the old witch cast a deep sleep over him, and he said to the young lady, “Let’s sit down and rest a little. I’m so tired I can’t stand any longer.” So they sat down, and he laid his head in her lap and fell asleep. While he slept, she took the cloak from his shoulders, hung it on her own, gathered up the diamonds, and wished herself home again.

He woke to find that his lady had tricked him and left him alone on the wild rock. “What roguery there is in this world!” he said, and he sat there in misery and fear, with no idea what to do. The rock was the home of fierce giants, and soon he saw three of them striding about. “My only hope is to pretend I’m asleep,” he thought, and he lay down as though he were sleeping soundly. The giants came up, and the first pushed him with his foot. “What’s this worm curled up here?” he said. “Stamp on him and kill him,” said the second. “Not worth the bother,” said the third. “Let him live. He’ll crawl higher up the mountain, and some cloud will roll in and carry him off.” And they moved on. But the huntsman had heard every word. As soon as they were gone, he climbed to the summit, and after he had sat there a little while, a cloud came rolling around him, swept him up in a whirlwind, and carried him along for some time, until it set down in a garden. He dropped softly to the ground among the greens and cabbages.

He looked around and said, “If I don’t find something to eat, I’ll be worse off than ever. I don’t see any apples or pears or fruit of any kind here, only vegetables.” Finally he told himself, “I could eat some salad. It would refresh me and give me strength.” So he picked a fine head and ate some of it. But he had barely swallowed two bites when he felt himself changing, and to his horror he saw that he had become a donkey. Still, he was very hungry, and the salad tasted good, so he kept eating until he reached a different kind of salad. He had hardly tasted it when another change came over him, and he saw, to his great luck, that he had his old shape back.

Then he lay down and slept off some of his weariness. The next morning when he woke, he picked a head each of the good salad and the bad, and he thought, “This will put me back on the road to fortune, and let me pay some people back for their treachery.” He set off to look for the castle of his friends, and after wandering for a few days he happened to find it. He stained his face brown all over, so that even his own mother would not have known him, then went into the castle and asked for a bed for the night. “I’m so tired I can’t go any farther,” he said. “Countryman,” said the witch, “who are you, and what brings you here?” “I’m a messenger,” he said. “The king sent me to find the finest salad that grows under the sun. I’ve been lucky enough to find it, and I have it with me. But the sun is so hot that it’s starting to wilt, and I don’t know whether I can carry it any farther.”

When the witch and the young lady heard about this wonderful salad, they were eager to taste it. “Dear countryman,” they said, “just let us have a taste.” “Of course,” he answered. “I have two heads of it with me, and I’ll give you one.” He opened his bag and handed them the bad one. The witch took it into the kitchen herself to be prepared. When it was ready, she couldn’t wait for it to be brought upstairs. She took a few leaves right away and put them in her mouth, and no sooner had she swallowed them than she lost her own shape and ran out into the courtyard, braying, as a donkey. Then the maid came into the kitchen, and when she saw the salad ready, she started to carry it up. On the way, though, she felt the same urge as the old woman to taste it, and she ate a few leaves. She too turned into a donkey and ran after the other, and the dish with the salad fell to the ground. All this time the messenger was sitting with the beautiful young lady. Since nobody came with the salad, and she was longing to taste it, she said, “I wonder where the salad is.” He guessed that something had happened and said, “I’ll go to the kitchen and see.” On his way he saw two donkeys running around in the courtyard, and the salad lying on the ground. “Good!” he said. “Those two have had their share.” He gathered up the rest of the leaves, put them on the dish, and brought them to the young lady. “I’ve brought the dish myself so you won’t have to wait any longer,” he said. She ate some, and like the others she ran off into the courtyard, braying.

Then the huntsman washed his face and went out into the courtyard so that they would recognize him. “Now you’ll pay for your roguery,” he said. He tied all three to a rope and led them along until he came to a mill, where he knocked at the window. “What is it?” said the miller. “I have three troublesome animals here,” said the huntsman. “If you’ll take them, give them food and a place to stay, and treat them the way I tell you, I’ll pay whatever you ask.” “Gladly,” said the miller, “but how am I to treat them?” The huntsman said, “Beat the old one three times a day and feed her hay once. Beat the next one, the maid, once a day and feed her hay three times. And the youngest, the beautiful lady, gets hay three times a day and no beatings.” He couldn’t bring himself to have her beaten. After that he went back to the castle, where he found everything he could want.

A few days later the miller came to him and said that the old donkey was dead. “The other two are alive and eating,” he said, “but they’re so miserable that they can’t last long.” The huntsman took pity on them. He told the miller to bring them back, and when they arrived, he gave them some of the good salad to eat. The beautiful young lady threw herself on her knees before him. “Dearest huntsman,” she said, “forgive me for all the harm I did you! My mother made me do it. It was against my will, for I always loved you dearly. Your wishing-cloak is hanging in the closet, and I’ll give you the bird’s heart as well.” But he said, “Keep it. It will come to the same thing, because I mean to make you my wife.” So they were married, and they lived happily together until they died.
